newsitem.title: USA: March U.S. vehicle sales surge despite Ford drop.
newsitem.headline: March U.S. vehicle sales surge despite Ford drop.

text.p: U.S. car and truck sales surged to the strongest level in more than a year during March despite a 2.6 percent sales decline reported by Ford Motor Co. on Thursday and a deceleration in Toyota Motor Corp.'s recent market share gains.

Americans bought cars and trucks at an annualized rate of 15.8 million units in March, up from 15.5 million a year earlier and 15.3 million in February -- an indication of strength that some analysts said may fuel inflation worries.

"It's a good number from a sales standpoint, but a not a good number from an auto stock standpoint," said investment bank J.P. Morgan auto analyst David Bradley. "In this market, strong sales mean the likelhood of the Fed raising (interest) rates is higher."
The last time industry sales sales reached an annualized rate of 15.8 million units was December 1995.
Total industry sales in March were up 1.4 percent over a year earlier to 1,396,392 light vehicles. For the first quarter of 1997, sales were up 2 percent to 3,642,288 units.

Scott Merlis, an independent auto analyst in Westport, Conn., said much of the sales strength was due to generous incentives that were drawing consumers into showrooms. Many sales may have been pulled forward, creating the risk that volume will taper off later in the year, he said.
Despite generous incentives, Ford reported a 9.5 percent decline in sales of North American-built passenger cars to 141,305.

In response, Ford said it will idle four North American car plants next week to help keep its dealer inventories from swelling. Plants in Kansas City, Mo.; Wayne, Mich.; Lorain, Ohio; and Cuautitlan, Mexico will not build small and mid-size cars, idling a total of 8,100 workers until April 14.

Ford's light truck sales, which include the strong-selling pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles that have powered most of the company's automotive profits in recent years, rose 3.5 percent to 201,142 units.

Detroit's No. 2 automaker said its first-quarter North American truck output was a record, up 8 percent over last year, despite a strike at a truck seat supplier. It predicted second-quarter truck output would be up 10 percent over the year-ago period, leading to another record.

"We've expanded our truck assembly capacity substantially in recent years and presently nearly all of our truck plants are operating on overtime schedules to keep pace with strong consumer demand," Ford said.
But Ford said some of its key car models posted declines, including the Taurus, which dropped 9.1 percent, and the Contour, which fell 16 percent.

At the end of the first quarter, the Taurus, with sales of 88,135 units, had relinquished its position as America's best-selling car to the Chevrolet Cavalier, which had sales of 91,189. Toyota's Camry was the third-best seller.
Overall, Ford sold 345,065 light vehicles in March vs. 354,105 a year earlier.
Toyota, which posted a 55.5 percent sales increase in January and a 17 percent increase in February, saw its sales gains slow to 5 percent, for a total of 121,741 cars and trucks.
Toyota's domestic car sales rose 4.1 percent, but the big story was import trucks, with sales of new entries such as the RAV4 and 4Runner sport utility vehicles up 23 percent.

Toyota's share of the U.S. car and light truck market rose to 8.7 percent from about 8.4 percent a year earlier, a much smaller increase than the 1.6 percentage points it has gained during the first three months of 1997.
General Motors Corp. Wednesday reported a 4.1 percent sales increase, due partly to new models and the fact that March 1996 truck sales were dragged down by a costly strike.

For the first time in months, GM reported a slight gain in market share, capturing 30.8 percent of the U.S. car and truck market, up from just over 30 percent in the year-ago period and the first two months of 1997.
Chrysler Corp. Tuesday reported its sales fell 3.4 percent, while Nissan Motor Co. Ltd. reported an 18.8 percent increase, and Honda Motor Co. Ltd. reported a 6.6 percent decline.

European automakers posted a combined 15.5 percent increase in sales to 50,346 units for the month, led by a 40 percent increase by Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG and a 30 percent increase from Mercedes-Benz AG -- gains analysts attribute to income growth and investment gains among the wealthy.
